docs.title: Plotting API
docs.text:
This page describes plotmux's public plotting functions: plotmux.hist, plotmux.bar, plotmux.stacked_bar, plotmux.cdf, plotmux.line, plotmux.scatter, plotmux.slope, plotmux.layer, and plotmux.grid. It explains the concepts shared by all of them: marks and panels, backends, the axes options, and the Figure object they all return.

Prerequisites: You'll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial. It is helpful to know a bit of NumPy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plotmux exposes nine top-level plotting functions:

  • plotmux.hist(): plot a histogram
  • plotmux.bar(): plot a bar chart
  • plotmux.stacked_bar(): plot a stacked bar chart
  • plotmux.cdf(): plot an empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF)
  • plotmux.line(): plot a line chart
  • plotmux.scatter(): plot a scatter chart
  • plotmux.slope(): plot a slope/abline reference line
  • plotmux.layer(): combine several charts onto one shared set of axes
  • plotmux.grid(): lay out several charts as independent panels in a grid

Each of these functions:

  1. builds a backend-agnostic mark (what is drawn: the data and its style, for example a HistogramSpec) and wraps it in a panel (one set of axes: a PanelSpec),
  2. renders that panel through a backend (Matplotlib, xy, ...), resolved from the backend argument or the current default backend (see Choosing a backend),
  3. returns the result wrapped in a Figure.

A backend only draws three primitives (bars, lines and points) and applies the axes style. The numbers on the screen (the bins of a histogram, the steps of a CDF, the stacking of a bar chart, the default colors) are decided once, before the backend is called, so the same call draws the same chart on every backend. Swapping the backend is a one-line change.

docs.title: Plotting a Histogram
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], bins=10, title="My histogram")
>>> fig.save("histogram.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

bins controls the number of histogram bins. xmin/xmax are the range of the values that are binned: each can be an explicit numeric value, a quantile string such as "q0.1" (the 10% quantile), or None to fall back to the min/max of values. They are not axis limits: the axes autoscale on the bars that are drawn.

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 100], bins=10, xmin="q0.0", xmax="q0.95")
>>> fig.save("histogram.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

Set density=True to normalize the histogram so the area under it integrates to 1.

docs.title: Plotting a Bar Chart
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.bar([1, 2, 3], [4, 9, 1], label="counts")
>>> fig.save("bar.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

width controls the width of each bar, in x data units (defaults to 0.8), on every backend. x can also be an array of strings (e.g. ["a", "b", "c"]), drawn as a categorical axis, in which case width is a fraction of the band of a category.

docs.title: Plotting a Stacked Bar Chart
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> from plotmux.specs import BarSeries
>>> fig = plotmux.stacked_bar(
...     ["Apples", "Pears", "Nectarines"],
...     [BarSeries(y=[2, 1, 4], label="2015"), BarSeries(y=[1, 3, 2], label="2016")],
... )
>>> fig.save("stacked_bar.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

stacked_bar() draws its series cumulatively: each BarSeries is stacked on top of the running total of the series before it (a plain cumulative sum, so negative values are not handled specially), at each x position. series is a list of plotmux.specs.BarSeries(y=..., label=None, color=None), one per stacked segment, in bottom-to-top order. A series with no explicit color gets the next color of plotmux.colors.DEFAULT_PALETTE (see Colors). A stacked bar chart works standalone, in a layer and in a grid on every backend.

docs.title: Plotting an Empirical CDF
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.cdf([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], title="My CDF")
>>> fig.save("cdf.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

plotmux.cdf() plots the exact empirical cumulative distribution function P(X <= x) of values. See Plotting a CDF for the binning option nbins and the range xmin/xmax. The ylabel defaults to "cumulative probability" instead of None.

docs.title: Plotting a Line Chart
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], label="y = x^2")
>>> fig.save("line.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

linewidth and linestyle ("solid", "dashed", "dotted", or "dashdot") control the line's appearance.

docs.title: Plotting a Scatter Chart
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], size=20)
>>> fig.save("scatter.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

size controls the marker size, edgecolor sets a separate color for the marker edge (None reuses color for the edge too), marker is one of "circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross" and "x", and fill=False draws hollow markers.

docs.title: Plotting a Slope / Abline
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.slope(2, 10, xmin=0, xmax=5)
>>> fig.save("slope.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

plotmux.slope(gradient, intercept=0.0, ...) draws a reference line, y = gradient * x + intercept. It has no data of its own, so it is drawn over the x extent of its panel: the xmin/xmax of the panel where they are set, else the extent of the data of the other marks of the panel. A panel with a slope and no extent raises an InvalidSpecError when it is built:

>>> import plotmux
>>> plotmux.slope(2, 10)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
plotmux.exceptions.InvalidSpecError: a mark needs the x extent of the panel (a slope has no data of its own): set xmin and xmax, or add a mark with numeric x data to the panel

The rule is the same on every backend, standalone, in a layer and in a grid. In a layer, the data of the siblings gives the extent, so a trend line over a scatter plot needs no xmin/xmax:

>>> import plotmux
>>> from plotmux.specs import SlopeSpec
>>> fig = plotmux.layer(
...     plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3, 4], [1.1, 2.0, 2.9, 4.2]),
...     SlopeSpec(gradient=1, intercept=0),
... )
>>> fig.save("scatter_with_trend.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

matplotlib and bokeh draw a slope as a native infinite line, which keeps extending when you zoom past the extent; the other backends draw the segment of the extent. See Layering Charts.

docs.title: Non-finite Values (NaN and inf)
docs.text:
The same input gives the same figure on every backend, so plotmux checks NaN and inf when the spec is built, not in the plotting library:

Input Result hist/cdf: NaN or inf among the values Dropped, with a UserWarning that gives the count (once per figure) hist/cdf: no finite value left InvalidSpecError hist/cdf: non-numeric values InvalidSpecError hist/cdf: a quantile bound (xmin="q0.1") Computed on the finite values line/scatter: NaN in x or y Kept: a gap in the line, no point line/scatter: inf or -inf in x or y InvalidSpecError a panel: a categorical x mixed with a numeric InvalidSpecError 
>>> import warnings
>>> import plotmux
>>> with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
...     warnings.simplefilter("always")
...     fig = plotmux.hist([1.0, 2.0, float("nan"), 3.0], bins=3)
...
>>> str(caught[0].message)
'HistogramSpec: 1 non-finite value(s) (NaN or inf) detected in values and filtered out'
>>> fig.spec.marks[0].values
array([1., 2., 3.])

InvalidSpecError is also a ValueError.

docs.title: Axes Options
docs.text:
hist, bar, stacked_bar, cdf, line, scatter, slope, and layer all accept the same axes options. They are declared once, as the typed dictionary plotmux.api.PanelOptions (and BoundedPanelOptions for the functions with xmin/xmax), and map to the fields of plotmux.specs.PanelSpec:

  • title: an optional axes title
  • xlabel / ylabel: optional axis labels
  • xscale / yscale: "linear" (default) or "log"
  • ymin / ymax: an optional explicit lower/upper limit of the y-axis. None leaves the axis autoscaled. They never accept a quantile string.
  • background_color: an optional axes background color, same format as color below. None uses the backend's default.
  • legend_title, legend_location, legend_orientation: the style of the legend, which exists if and only if at least one mark has a label. legend_location is one of "top_left", "top_right", "bottom_left", "bottom_right", "top", "bottom", "left" and "right" (there is no "best": three backends have no automatic placement, and None uses the default of the library). legend_orientation is "vertical" or "horizontal".
  • backend: the name of the backend to render with, or None for the current default (see Choosing a Backend)

bar, stacked_bar, line, scatter, slope and layer also accept xmin/xmax, the explicit limits of the x-axis. hist and cdf do not: their xmin/xmax are the range of the data they bin or plot.

Every chart type that draws a mark also accepts:

  • color: a hex string ("#rrggbb" or "#rrggbbaa"), a CSS/Matplotlib named color (e.g. "tab:blue"), or an RGB(A) tuple of floats in [0, 1]. None takes the next color of the default palette, so the color of a chart is the same on every backend. See Colors for details.
  • label: a label used in the legend
  • alpha: an optional opacity in [0, 1]. None uses the backend's default (usually fully opaque).
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.line(
...     [1, 2, 3],
...     [1, 4, 9],
...     color="tab:orange",
...     alpha=0.8,
...     label="y",
...     title="Quadratic",
...     xlabel="x",
...     ylabel="y",
...     yscale="log",
...     background_color="white",
...     legend_location="top_left",
...     ymin=1,
... )
>>> fig.save("line.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

A few fields only make sense for one chart type and live only on that function: bins/density (hist), width (bar/stacked_bar), nbins (cdf), linewidth/linestyle (line/slope), size/edgecolor/marker/fill (scatter), gradient/intercept (slope), series (stacked_bar).

plotmux.grid() accepts no axes option: each panel keeps its own. It takes only title (shown once above the whole grid), ncols, and backend. See Grid Layouts.

docs.title: Unknown Keyword Arguments
docs.text:
There is no keyword pass-through to the plotting library: a call means the same on every backend. A misspelled or library-specific keyword is a TypeError of plotmux at the call site:

>>> import plotmux
>>> plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], histtype="step")
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: hist() got an unexpected keyword argument 'histtype'. The axes options are: ...

To set an option of the library, modify the native figure after the render with Figure.to_native() (see The Figure Object).

docs.title: Choosing a Backend
docs.text: This page describes how plotmux resolves which rendering backend to use, how to change the default backend, and how to add a new one.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A backend turns a backend-agnostic spec into a plotting library's native figure object (e.g. a Matplotlib Figure), and knows how to export that native object to a file. plotmux ships with five built-in backends:

  • "matplotlib": renders with Matplotlib (the default). Requires the matplotlib extra.
  • "xy": renders with xy. Requires the xy extra.
  • "bokeh": renders with Bokeh. Requires the bokeh extra. Only the "html" export format is supported: static image export (png/svg) would additionally require a Selenium webdriver at runtime, which is outside the scope of a pip install bokeh.
  • "altair": renders with Altair (Vega-Lite). Requires the altair extra. Only the "html"/"json" export formats are supported: static image export (png/svg/pdf) would additionally require the vl-convert-python package, which is outside the scope of a pip install altair.
  • "plotly": renders with Plotly. Requires the plotly extra. Only the "html"/"json" export formats are supported: static image export (png/svg/pdf) would additionally require the kaleido package, which is outside the scope of a pip install plotly.

A backend is only imported when it is used, so importing plotmux never fails because a backend's dependency is missing; only calling a plotting function that needs it does (it raises a BackendNotFoundError that names the extra to install).

docs.title: Selecting a Backend per Call
docs.text:
Every plotting function accepts a backend argument:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5, backend="matplotlib")
>>> fig.save("histogram.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

backend=None (the default) uses the current default backend.

docs.title: Setting the Default Backend
docs.text:
plotmux.set_backend() changes the default backend for the current thread/task:

>>> import plotmux
>>> plotmux.set_backend("matplotlib")

docs.title: Temporarily Overriding the Default Backend
docs.text:
plotmux.backend() is a context manager that overrides the default backend for the duration of a with block, then restores the previous default:

>>> import plotmux
>>> with plotmux.backend("matplotlib"):
...     fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3])

This is useful to render the same plotting code with several backends, e.g. to compare their output, without permanently changing the default:

>>> import plotmux
>>> for name in ["matplotlib"]:  # doctest: +SKIP
...     with plotmux.backend(name):
...         plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9]).save(f"line_{name}.png")

The default backend is stored in a contextvars.ContextVar, so it is thread/task-local: setting it in one thread or asyncio task never leaks into, or races with, another one, while still behaving like a single process-wide default in the common single-threaded case.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
plotmux.set_backend()/plotmux.backend() reject an unknown name immediately, at the call site, before storing it — this catches a typo like "mtaplotlib" right away instead of only on the next plotting call, at zero import cost:

>>> import plotmux
>>> plotmux.set_backend("not_a_backend")  # doctest: +SKIP
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
RuntimeError: Unknown backend 'not_a_backend'. Known backends: ['altair', 'bokeh', 'matplotlib', 'plotly', 'xy']

A name that passes this check (a built-in name, or one advertised by an installed third-party plugin) can still fail later, when a plotting function actually renders with it, if its underlying library turns out not to be installed — being known is not the same as being installed (plotmux.backends.available_backends() lists the backends that can be used). Passing such a name directly to a plotting function's backend argument (bypassing set_backend/backend) raises the same error there instead:

>>> import plotmux
>>> plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], backend="not_a_backend")  # doctest: +SKIP
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
RuntimeError: No backend registered under the name 'not_a_backend'. ...

docs.title: Adding a Third-Party Backend
docs.text:
A backend is a class with three required methods: capabilities(), draw(scene) and save(native, path, fmt). It draws the three primitives of a scene and applies the axes style; it does not decide any number on the screen. plotmux.scene.build_scene(spec) turns the spec of a figure into an AxesScene (one axes) or a GridScene (a grid of axes): its primitives are Bars, Line and Points (see plotmux.primitives), each with its resolved color and label, and the AxesScene holds the title, the labels, the scales, the limits, the background color, the legend style and the categories of the x-axis.

A separate package can add a new backend without modifying plotmux's source, via the plotmux.backends entry-point group. The entry point is named after the backend, and its value is package.module:BackendClass:

[project.entry-points."plotmux.backends"]
my_backend = "my_package.plotmux_backend:MyBackend"

# my_package/plotmux_backend.py
from plotmux.backends.base import Backend, BackendCapabilities
from plotmux.primitives import Bars, Line, Points
from plotmux.scene import AxesScene, GridScene


class MyBackend(Backend):
    name = "my_backend"

    def capabilities(self) -> BackendCapabilities:
        return BackendCapabilities(
            name=self.name,
            formats=frozenset({"png"}),  # the export formats of a figure
            grid_formats=frozenset({"png"}),  # the export formats of a grid
            legend_locations=frozenset({"top_left", "top_right"}),
            markers=frozenset({"circle", "square"}),
        )

    def draw(self, scene: AxesScene | GridScene):
        # Draw each primitive of scene.primitives (Bars, Line or Points), then apply the
        # style of the axes. A GridScene holds one AxesScene per panel in scene.panels.
        ...

    def save(self, native, path, fmt): ...

    # Optional: how `Figure.show()` displays the native figure (the default raises
    # `NotImplementedError`), and the rich display of Jupyter (the default uses the
    # `_repr_mimebundle_` or `_repr_html_`/`_repr_svg_`/`_repr_png_`/`_repr_jpeg_` of `native`).
    def show(self, native): ...

    def mimebundle(self, native): ...

Backend.render(spec) is not overridden: it builds the scene, checks it against capabilities() (a legend location or a marker that the backend does not declare raises an UnsupportedSpecError before anything is drawn, and plotmux.export.save raises an UnsupportedFormatError for a format that is not declared before any file or directory is created), then calls draw. A new chart type needs no change in a backend when it is a composition of Bars, Line and Points, see the developer guide.

The module is imported, and the class instantiated once, the first time the name is used (e.g. plotmux.hist(..., backend="my_backend")). import plotmux reads no entry point and imports no backend: none of the five built-in backends (matplotlib, xy, bokeh, altair, plotly) is imported before it is requested either. plotmux.set_backend("my_backend") accepts the name as soon as the package is installed, because the names of the entry points are read from the installed metadata without importing the plugin.

A backend can also be registered from code, with register_backend:

>>> from plotmux.backends import get_backend, register_backend
>>> from plotmux.backends.matplotlib.backend import MatplotlibBackend
>>> class OtherBackend(MatplotlibBackend):
...     name = "other_backend"
...
>>> register_backend(OtherBackend())
>>> get_backend("other_backend") is get_backend("other_backend")
True

A name already used by a registered backend or by a built-in backend is refused with a BackendRegistrationError, so installing a plugin never takes over matplotlib by accident. To replace a backend on purpose, call register_backend(backend, replace=True). An instance registered that way wins over the built-in backend and over a plugin of the same name.

If the library of a backend is not installed, using the backend raises a BackendNotFoundError that names the extra to install (e.g. pip install "plotmux[matplotlib]"), and the original ImportError is its __cause__. plotmux.backends.available_backends() lists the names that can be used, without importing anything. Any other exception raised while a plugin loads (a bug in the plugin) is not hidden: it propagates when the plugin is first used.

docs.title: Plotting a CDF
docs.text: This page describes plotmux.cdf(), which plots the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of an array of values.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plotmux.cdf() plots P(X <= x): the fraction of values that fall at or below each point on the x-axis. The curve is exact, a step of 1 / n at each of the n values, and it is the same on every backend:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.cdf([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], title="My CDF")
>>> fig.save("cdf.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

The curve has 2 n vertices, so a very large input draws a large polyline.

docs.title: Binning Large Inputs
docs.text:
nbins is an opt-in binning that bounds the number of vertices to 2 * nbins + 1: the values are binned first, over their own range, and the curve is the cumulative sum of the bins. None (the default) is the exact CDF:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.cdf([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], nbins=20)
>>> fig.save("cdf.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

docs.title: Range
docs.text:
xmin/xmax restrict the part of the curve that is drawn, with the same semantics as plotmux.hist(): each can be an explicit numeric value, a quantile string such as "q0.1" (the 10% quantile, computed on the finite values), or None to fall back to the min/max of values. They do not renormalize the curve: the height of the curve at x is still the fraction of all the values at or below x.

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.cdf([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 100], xmin="q0.0", xmax="q0.95")
>>> fig.save("cdf.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

They are not axis limits either: the axes autoscale on the drawn curve. Set ymin/ymax to limit the y-axis.

docs.title: Style Arguments
docs.text:
cdf accepts the same options as hist, line, and scatter: title, xlabel, ylabel, xscale, yscale, color, alpha, label, background_color, ymin, ymax, the legend options and backend (see Axes Options). The one difference is ylabel, which defaults to "cumulative probability" instead of None, since a CDF's y-axis always represents that same quantity unless you override it:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.cdf([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], ylabel="fraction of samples")
>>> fig.save("cdf.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: This page describes plotmux.colors, which lets every color argument in the unified API accept the same set of color formats, regardless of the backend rendering the figure.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every color argument in plotmux (plotmux.hist(..., color=...), plotmux.line(..., color=...), plotmux.scatter(..., color=...), plotmux.bar(..., color=...)) accepts one of:

  • a hex string, "#rrggbb" or "#rrggbbaa"
  • a CSS or Matplotlib named color, e.g. "tab:blue", "crimson"
  • an RGB(A) tuple of floats in [0, 1]

Internally, parse_color() normalizes any of these into one canonical representation, an RGBA tuple of floats in [0, 1]. Each backend then converts that canonical tuple to whatever its native call expects. This lookup table is bundled with plotmux itself (it mirrors Matplotlib's own BASE_COLORS, TABLEAU_COLORS, and CSS4_COLORS tables), so named colors resolve correctly even when Matplotlib is not installed, e.g. when using the xy backend alone.

docs.title: Parsing a Color
docs.text:
>>> from plotmux.colors import parse_color
>>> parse_color("#ff0000")
(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)
>>> parse_color("tab:blue")
(0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765, 1.0)
>>> parse_color((0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0)

An invalid color raises a ValueError:

>>> from plotmux.colors import parse_color
>>> parse_color("not-a-color")  # doctest: +SKIP
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: ...

docs.title: Using Colors in a Plot
docs.text:
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], color="#1f77b4")
>>> fig.save("line.png")  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> fig = plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], color=(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.8))
>>> fig.save("scatter.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

A spec normalizes its color field to the canonical RGBA representation as soon as it is constructed, so every backend always receives an already-validated color and never has to parse a raw color itself.

docs.title: Predefined Colors and the Default Palette
docs.text:
plotmux.colors also exposes a small set of predefined colors, each already a parse_color-normalized RGBA tuple:

>>> from plotmux.colors import PRIMARY, SECONDARY, TERTIARY
>>> PRIMARY
(0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765, 1.0)

DEFAULT_PALETTE is an ordered tuple of RGBA tuples used to assign successive, visually-distinct colors to multiple series, or to plotmux.layer() children that set no explicit color:

>>> from plotmux.colors import DEFAULT_PALETTE
>>> len(DEFAULT_PALETTE)
10

docs.title: The Figure Object
docs.text: This page describes Figure, the object returned by every plotmux plotting function, and how to display, save, or escape to the native figure it wraps.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plotmux.hist(), plotmux.cdf(), plotmux.line(), plotmux.scatter(), plotmux.bar(), plotmux.stacked_bar(), plotmux.slope(), plotmux.layer(), and plotmux.grid() all return a Figure. It keeps three things together:

  • spec: the backend-agnostic spec that was rendered
  • backend_name: the name of the backend that rendered it
  • native: the backend's native figure object (e.g. a Matplotlib Figure)
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5)
>>> fig.backend_name
'matplotlib'

docs.title: Displaying a Figure
docs.text:
Figure.show() displays the figure using the backend's default viewer:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5)
>>> fig.show()  # doctest: +SKIP

If the native object does not support .show(), a NotImplementedError is raised.

docs.title: Saving a Figure
docs.text:
Figure.save() saves the figure to a file. The export format is inferred from the file suffix (e.g. .png, .svg, .pdf), and the parent directory is created automatically if it doesn't already exist:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5)
>>> fig.save("output/histogram.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

A path with no suffix raises a ValueError, since the export format cannot be inferred. Supported formats depend on the backend:

Backend Supported formats matplotlib png, svg, pdf, jpg, jpeg xy png, jpg, jpeg, webp, svg, pdf, html bokeh html altair html, json plotly html, json

One exception to this table: a plotmux.grid(..., backend="xy") figure only supports "html", even though the xy backend otherwise supports the full row above. xy has no primitive for composing arbitrary, already-built panels side by side, so a grid is laid out at export time as sandboxed HTML iframes rather than a rasterizable native object; see Grid Layouts for details. The formats of a grid are declared apart from those of a single panel (BackendCapabilities.grid_formats).

Requesting an unsupported format raises an UnsupportedFormatError (also a ValueError) that names the backend and lists the formats it supports, before any file or directory is created. Check fig.supported_formats ahead of time to avoid relying on that error for control flow:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5, backend="matplotlib")
>>> sorted(fig.supported_formats)
['jpeg', 'jpg', 'pdf', 'png', 'svg']

plotmux.export.save() is the underlying function called by Figure.save(), if you need to call it directly with a Figure you already have.

docs.title: Displaying a Figure in Jupyter
docs.text:
Figure displays itself automatically as the last expression of a Jupyter cell, so no extra call is needed beyond leaving fig as a cell's last expression. The display comes from the backend that rendered the figure (Backend.mimebundle): a PNG for matplotlib, and the HTML or mime bundle of the native object for the other backends. Figure forwards no other attribute to the native object, so a typo like fig.sav(...) raises a plain AttributeError.

fig.show() displays the figure with the viewer of its backend, and works on every backend: matplotlib opens a window (pyplot.show), bokeh calls bokeh.io.show, altair and plotly call the show of their native figure, and xy opens the HTML of the figure in the web browser.

docs.title: Escaping to the Native Figure
docs.text:
Figure.to_native() returns the backend's native figure object, the escape hatch to reach backend-specific functionality not exposed by the unified API:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.hist([1, 2, 3], bins=5)
>>> mpl_fig = fig.to_native()  # a matplotlib.figure.Figure

Use this when you need a backend-specific feature that plotmux's unified API does not cover, rather than growing the common API to the union of every backend.

docs.title: Checking What a Backend Supports Ahead of Time
docs.text:
A backend declares what it supports as data, in its BackendCapabilities: the export formats of a figure and of a grid, the legend locations and the scatter markers. Every chart type works standalone, in a layer and in a grid on every backend, so the differences between the backends are only these four sets. plotmux.backends.capabilities() answers without triggering the failure:

>>> import plotmux
>>> caps = plotmux.backends.capabilities("altair")
>>> caps.name
'altair'
>>> sorted(caps.formats)
['html', 'json']
>>> sorted(caps.markers)
['circle', 'cross', 'diamond', 'square', 'triangle', 'x']

A request outside these sets (a legend location or a marker that the backend does not honor) raises an UnsupportedSpecError naming the backend and the supported values, before anything is drawn, instead of being silently ignored.

docs.title: Grid Layouts
docs.text: This page describes plotmux.grid(), which lays out several charts as independent panels in a grid.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plotmux.grid() accepts any number of panels, marks, or single-panel Figures, and lays each one out in its own, independent panel (the backend-agnostic equivalent of Matplotlib's pyplot.subplots()). This is different from plotmux.layer(), which draws every item onto one shared set of axes: with grid, each item keeps its own axes.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import plotmux
>>> from plotmux.specs import HistogramSpec
>>> fig = plotmux.grid(
...     HistogramSpec(values=np.arange(101), bins=10),
...     plotmux.line([0, 100], [0, 5], title="a line"),
...     ncols=2,
...     title="Two independent panels",
... )
>>> fig.save("grid.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

A mark (such as the histogram above) is wrapped in a default panel. A Figure passed as an item, such as plotmux.line(...) above, contributes its panel with its own title, labels, scales and limits. The earlier native figure is discarded and everything is re-rendered together.

A panel may hold several marks, since layering and gridding are independent, composable concerns: a panel can contain several series sharing one set of axes, whatever the marks (a slope and a stacked bar included):

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.grid(
...     plotmux.layer(plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]), plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])),
...     plotmux.slope(1, 0, xmin=0, xmax=3),
...     ncols=2,
... )
>>> len(fig.spec.panels)
2

docs.title: Arranging Panels
docs.text:
ncols controls the number of columns. Panels fill left to right, top to bottom, in the order the items were given; the last row is left short (its remaining panels left empty) when the number of items is not a multiple of ncols:

>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.grid(
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]),
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1]),
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9]),
...     ncols=2,
... )
>>> fig.save("grid.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

docs.title: Style Arguments
docs.text:
Unlike hist, line, scatter, and layer, grid only accepts title and backend, plus ncols. title is shown once above the whole grid, not any individual panel. xlabel, ylabel, xscale, yscale, and color have no meaning at the grid level since each panel keeps its own style: set those on the panels themselves instead (a misspelled or unsupported keyword is a TypeError).

The legend and the plot background are per panel on matplotlib, bokeh, altair and xy. plotly has one legend per figure, so a grid takes the legend style of its first panel that has a legend; the background of a panel is a rectangle below its traces.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text: A grid holds panels, and a panel holds marks, so a grid cannot be nested in the type: passing a GridSpec (or a Figure built from one) as one of the items raises an InvalidSpecError. grid also requires at least one item, and ncols must be a positive integer.

docs.title: The xy Backend Is HTML-Only for Grids
docs.text: xy has no primitive for arranging arbitrary, already-built, independent panels side by side (its facet_chart repeats one fixed chart per value of a data column, which is a different thing), so grid(..., backend="xy") lays out each panel's standalone chart as a sandboxed HTML <iframe> at export time instead of producing a single rasterizable native figure. As a result, fig.save(...) only accepts an .html path for an xy grid, and every other format raises an UnsupportedFormatError before any file or directory is created. This is declared in Backend.capabilities().grid_formats, and fig.supported_formats of a grid reads it. Every other backend supports its full usual set of formats for grid() too. See The Figure Object for the full per-backend format table.

docs.title: Layering Charts
docs.text: This page describes plotmux.layer(), which combines several charts onto one shared set of axes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
plotmux.layer() accepts any number of marks, or single-panel Figures, and draws them together on one shared set of axes, e.g. overlaying a line on top of a histogram. A layer is a panel with several marks:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import plotmux
>>> from plotmux.specs import HistogramSpec
>>> fig = plotmux.layer(
...     HistogramSpec(values=np.arange(101), bins=10),
...     plotmux.line([0, 100], [0, 5]),
...     title="Histogram with a reference line",
... )
>>> fig.save("layered.png")  # doctest: +SKIP

A Figure passed as an item, such as plotmux.line(...) above, contributes its marks and its axes options. The earlier native figure is discarded and everything is re-rendered together, since two independent native figures can't be merged after the fact.

docs.title: Axes Options
docs.text:
Like hist, line, and scatter, layer accepts the axes options (title, xlabel, ylabel, xscale, yscale, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, background_color, the legend options and backend, see The Plotting API). They describe the combined axes.

The axes options of the figures given as items are merged, in this order:

  1. an option set in the call to layer wins;
  2. else the unique value of the figures that is not the default;
  3. else, if two figures have different values, an InvalidSpecError asks you to set the option in the call.
>>> import plotmux
>>> fig = plotmux.layer(
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], title="a trend"),
...     plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3], [1.1, 1.9, 3.2]),
... )
>>> fig.spec.title
'a trend'
>>> plotmux.layer(
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], title="a"),
...     plotmux.line([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1], title="b"),
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
plotmux.exceptions.InvalidSpecError: the figures have different values of title: ['a', 'b']. Set title in the call to layer.

docs.title: Layering a Slope with a Data-Bound Chart
docs.text:
SlopeSpec (a reference/trend line with no data of its own, see The Plotting API) is drawn over the x extent of the panel, so it works in any layer, on every backend, as long as the panel has an extent: the data of another mark, or xmin/xmax. Give it as a mark, not as the figure of plotmux.slope() (which needs its own xmin/xmax):

>>> import plotmux
>>> from plotmux.specs import SlopeSpec
>>> fig = plotmux.layer(
...     plotmux.scatter([1, 2, 3, 4], [1.1, 2.0, 2.9, 4.2]),
...     SlopeSpec(gradient=1, intercept=0),
...     backend="altair",
... )
>>> fig.save("scatter_with_trend.html")  # doctest: +SKIP

A layer with a slope and nothing else raises an InvalidSpecError when the panel is built, whatever the backend, because there is nothing to compute an extent from.

docs.title: Colors in a Layer
docs.text: A mark that sets no explicit color is assigned one from DEFAULT_PALETTE (see Colors), in draw order, so each mark remains visually distinguishable without you having to pick colors by hand. A mark with an explicit color does not use a color of the palette.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text: A layer holds marks, and a mark is not a panel, so layers do not nest in the type: passing a layer as an item of another layer simply contributes its marks. Passing a grid raises an InvalidSpecError. A categorical x (strings) cannot be mixed with a numeric x on the same axes, and layer requires at least one item.

  • Grid Layouts: lay out several charts (or layers) as independent panels in a grid
  • Colors: how colors are assigned to the marks of a layer

docs.title: Migrating to the Primitives-Based Design
docs.text:
This page lists the breaking changes of the core-model redesign (see DESIGN.md) and how to update your code. It is the source of the migration section of the release notes. There is no alias, no deprecation period and no shim: the old names are gone.

The short version: a spec is now a mark plus a panel. The figure-level fields (title, labels, scales, limits, background, legend) moved from every chart spec to PanelSpec, a layer is a panel with several marks, and a backend only draws three primitives.

docs.title: Using the Plotting Functions
docs.text:
The nine functions keep their names and their arguments. Five things change:

Before After plotmux.hist(x, histtype="step"): extra keywords go to the library A TypeError of plotmux: hist() got an unexpected keyword argument 'histtype'. Modify the native figure with fig.to_native() instead. xmin/xmax of hist/cdf were documented as the x-axis range (and set the limits of a CDF) xmin/xmax of hist and cdf are the range of the data; they are not axis limits. Use xmin/xmax of line, bar, ... or of layer for limits plotmux.cdf(x): a binned CDF (10 or 100 bins, depending on the backend), renormalized by xmin/xmax The exact empirical P(X <= x); nbins is an opt-in binning; xmin/xmax cut the curve without renormalizing it plotmux.slope(2, 1) standalone on matplotlib and bokeh only plotmux.slope(2, 1, xmin=0, xmax=10) on every backend; a slope needs an x extent legend_location="best" Removed: three backends have no automatic placement. Use None for the default of the library

Also:

  • The first color of a chart is now the first color of DEFAULT_PALETTE on every backend (it was the default color of the library).
  • layer(...) merges the axes options of the figures it is given (see Layering Charts): the title and the labels of a figure used to be dropped silently. Two figures with different non-default values of an option now raise an InvalidSpecError; set the option in the call to layer.
  • stacked_bar works in a layer and in a grid, and slope in a grid, on every backend.
  • legend_title, legend_location and legend_orientation are now keyword arguments of every plotting function (they were only fields of the specs).
  • fig.supported_formats of a grid reads the formats of the grid (html only for xy).
  • A format that a backend does not support raises an UnsupportedFormatError before any file or directory is created.

docs.title: Using the Specs
docs.text: Before After HistogramSpec(values=v, title="t", xscale="log") PanelSpec(marks=(HistogramSpec(values=v),), title="t", xscale="log") LayerSpec(layers=(a, b), title="t") PanelSpec(marks=(a, b), title="t"); a layer is a panel with several marks GridSpec(cells=(a, b), ncols=2) where a cell is a spec or a layer GridSpec(panels=(PanelSpec(marks=(a,)), PanelSpec(marks=(b,))), ncols=2) BaseSpec, XBoundSpec MarkSpec (label, color, alpha) and PanelSpec (the axes style and the limits) fig.spec is the spec that was rendered fig.spec is a PanelSpec or a GridSpec; the marks are in fig.spec.marks StackedBarSpec(..., label=..., color=...) The label and the color are set on each BarSeries; setting them on the spec raises CdfSpec(..., ylabel=...) (the default "cumulative probability") The default is set by plotmux.cdf; a PanelSpec has ylabel=None by default Specs compared by identity, arrays aliased Specs are immutable and compare by value; arrays are copied and read-only plotmux.specs.check_equal_length plotmux.utils.to_paired_arrays plotmux.utils.compute_cdf_steps plotmux.utils.cdf_steps (exact CDF) plotmux.utils.slope.resolve_slope_xrange Removed: the x extent is PanelSpec.x_extent()

docs.title: Writing a Backend
docs.text:
The contract of a third-party backend changed (see Adding a Third-Party Backend).

Before After render(spec, **kwargs) dispatched on the type of the spec draw(scene): draw Bars, Line and Points, and apply the axes style; render is concrete supported_formats, _RENDERERS and _CAVEATS class attributes capabilities() returns a BackendCapabilities (formats, grid_formats, legend_locations, markers) make_renderer, resolve_renderer, check_export_format Removed: the base class checks the scene and export.save checks the format A module per spec type, per layer and per grid backend.py and style.py The entry point value was a module that registered a backend at import The value is package.module:BackendClass; there is no import-time side effect A new chart type needed a renderer in every backend A new chart type is a MarkSpec with to_primitives, with no backend change

docs.title: Checking What a Backend Supports
docs.text: plotmux.backends.capabilities(name) returns the formats, the legend locations and the markers of a backend. The old spec_types and caveats are gone: every chart type works standalone, in a layer and in a grid on every backend.
